entries: Behaviour assessment and training plans｜Understand the animal before deciding the plan｜Assess the animal's temperament, ability and suitability for training and find out its age, health and previous training history; the specific objectives and training methods depend on one's own actual training, duties and institutional procedures, and this page only describes the tasks.

Delivery of basic and advanced training｜Shaping behaviour step by step with signals｜Using commands, hand signals, reins, spurs and similar cues to guide the animal step by step to the target behaviour, training to the established standards of a performance or competition, and correcting bad habits such as kicking, breaking loose or resisting saddling.

Specialist training｜Divided by use｜Training horses for riding, harness work, performance or racing; training dogs for assistance tasks (including guide dogs and service dogs) or property protection; and training animals to carry goods or work as part of a pack team.

Animal care and health observation｜Keeping the animal in condition｜Feeding, exercise, cleaning and maintaining the training and keeping areas, observing the animal's physical condition to find problems that need medical attention, and administering medication as prescribed.

values: A/B/C: complete fictional materials

A behaviour observation: the same fictional dog, the same doorbell situation, for five consecutive days; each time only whether the dog jumped up within 10 seconds of the doorbell is recorded, and opportunities not observed are not filled in as zero. Day 1: 10 observations, 8 jumps; day 2: 10 and 7; day 3: 8 and 4; day 4: 10 and 3; day 5: 6 and 2. The visitors, the owner's responses and the distances were not standardised across the days; the number of unobserved opportunities, health, medication and other behaviours are all unknown.

B summary draft: "Ten days have been observed, 50 occasions in total, 24 jumps, a proportion of 48%; it decreased steadily day by day, so the reward method has been proven effective." A records no training method or reward and no control was set.

C client promise: "All behaviour problems have been cured, and it is guaranteed that the dog will not jump up again over the next seven days, with no need to check safety or health again." This material is a fictional editorial draft with no real client or animal.
Task: recompute and rewrite

List each of the five days' number of observations, number of jumps and proportion; the overall proportion uses the total jumps divided by the total observations, and the daily proportions must not be averaged or unobserved records filled in.

Check B item by item for the number of days, the counts, the proportion, the monotonic change and the causal claim about the method; check C item by item for the cure, the word all, the guarantee and the claim that no further checking is needed. Retain what is not known.

Write three client sentences: the first gives the results already observed; the second states the limitations of the change and the causal claim; the third gives the actual safety and health checks and the boundaries of authorization. This is paper review only, with no design or carrying out of animal training.
Reference answer: 24 out of 44

The five daily proportions are 80%, 70%, 50%, 30% and 33.33% (shown to two decimals); the totals are 44 and 24, and 24/44 = 54.55%. Day 5 is higher than day 4, so it cannot be written as decreasing steadily day by day. The unobserved opportunities are unknown, and the overall daily behaviour proportion cannot be inferred.

B's "ten days / 50 occasions / 48% / decreasing steadily day by day / reward proven effective" are all unsupported by A; A only observed five days and has no method record, standardised conditions or control, so training causality cannot be proven. C's claims about curing everything, seven-day guarantees and no further checks are all unsupported by the materials.

Three example sentences: "Over five days, 44 doorbell opportunities were observed, of which 24 involved jumping up, a proportion of 54.55%." "The daily proportions are 80/70/50/30/33.33%, the conditions were not standardised and no training method was recorded, so causality cannot be confirmed or future results guaranteed." "The real safety, health and task conditions must be checked separately by personnel with the corresponding duties, and a training identity does not confer diagnostic and treatment authority."
Boundary: paper review only
All of A/B/C is fictional and fully given; no real animals, client information, medical records or internal documents are used, and no additional materials are needed.

The pieces can show preparation in calculation, traceability and accurate communication; they are not animal handling, training effects, psychological suitability, hiring or a skill level assessment, and the paper conclusions must not be treated as treatment or a real training plan.

Client communication and teaching｜Passing the method on｜Explaining the training principles and homework to animal owners, teaching owners to train their own dogs, teaching visually impaired people to work with guide dogs, and organising or giving animal performances; the animal welfare explanation and on-site methods are checked against the actual post. — 25/100; weight=1/3; animal-trainers.profile.responsibilities-block.1[5]
